new:
changed with a 4% chance. 500 generations, a random start, errors of both kinds, 30 runs at each rate. Still not his: payoffs are exact where his are played out (one match of 200 rounds a pair, as far as the paper says), and games end at random after 200 rounds on average where his last exactly 200.

The paper gives the scheme a paragraph and a figure, and in six places I had to choose. (1) What a string is made of. The paper gives each element "a 4% independent chance of mutation, which implies an expectation of 1 element-mutation per string", so a string has 25 elements; that they are eight moves, sixteen arrows and the start state is my guess. (2) How many elements change. The text has each element changed with a 4% chance; Figure 3 says "switching one element at random". I followed the text, which is nearly word for word from Miller (1996), whose approach he says he uses, and Miller is plain that each place has its own chance. (3) How the pairs are drawn. The paper says only "with the probabilities biased by their scores". I took chances in proportion to the raw score; Miller draws in proportion to a normalised score (the score less the mean, over the standard deviation, plus 2, cut off at zero). (4) Which of a pair is copied. It is "the better performer" in the text and "the winner of the pair's match" in Figure 3; I took the one with the higher total score. (5) Ties for the twentieth place. The paper is silent. In `elite.py` the machine listed first wins and the twenty kept are listed first, so a newcomer never displaces a kept machine that scores exactly what it scores; and with exact payoffs a newcomer that behaves as a kept machine does scores exactly what that machine scores. With payoffs played out, as his are, such ties hardly arise once there are errors. (6) What makes a machine "the winner" of a run. The paper does not say. Mine is the commonest machine over the last 100 generations, as in the first run. None of the other readings was tried under seal.
why: The section presents 25 elements, the 4% rule, the proportional draw, the better of a pair and the commonest machine as his scheme. The paper does not state the first, speaks with two voices on the second and fourth (text against Figure 3), and is silent on the rest. The tie rule is not mentioned anywhere in the note. Miller (1996, pp. 94 to 99 and footnotes 6 and 7, read from the scan on disk) is where Ioannou's wording comes from.

The two writings differ in one
thing, the mutation. Mine changes elements of an eight-state string, as the paper describes, so about a third of newcomers are

new: The two writings differ in the mutation, and in how ties for the twentieth place are broken (the reader's at random, mine in favour of the machine listed first). Mine changes elements of an eight-state string, as the paper's text describes, so about a third of newcomers (36%) are unchanged copies and changes in states a machine does not use are carried along. The reader's minimises each machine and applies my study's mutation once, which works only on the states a machine uses and can add or remove a state. It does not always change something: by the second reader's count 24, 44, 43 and 63% of its newcomers at the four error rates were the same machine as their parent, against 49, 53, 58 and 67% of mine.
why: Three things. The scripts differ in tie-breaking too (`check_elitist.py` rounds to 8 places and shuffles; `elite.py` uses a stable sort). "As the paper describes" hides that Figure 3 says one element. And the study's `mutate()` does not always change something: it redraws an arrow to any state including the one it had, most of its moves do nothing to a one-state machine, and many changes vanish when the machine is minimised. The shares are counted over all newcomers in replays that reproduce `elite_run.json` and `elite_after.json` field for field (`replay_summary.out`).

What they show. (a) His result at 2%, Always-Defect the winner in 19 runs of 30, appears under no reading tried: all-defect leads 0 to 10 runs of 30 there in all seventeen batches. (b) At 4% my 20 against his 22 holds with exact payoffs whatever else is changed (17 to 23 runs in ten batches) and not with matches played out once, as the paper has them: there all-defect leads 8 to 16 runs of 30 in six batches, and the mean payoff is 1.61 to 1.99 against his 1.45. Brought nearer to his paper, my writing gives less of his high-error result. (c) How ties are broken seems to matter at 2%: 0 and 5 runs of 30 against 9 and 9 (p = 0.005), and mean payoffs of 2.47 and 2.33 against 2.07 and 2.13. (d) Neither twice and three times the mutation rate nor one element switched in every newcomer favours all-defect in my writing. His footnote 7 says that in his algorithm higher rates favour it hugely; and the difference from the reader's kind of mutation is then not how often a newcomer is changed. (e) Cooperation falls at each step of the error rate in every batch, and the handshake leads 2 to 11 runs of 30 at 1% in every batch. (f) Counted in the last generation only, as the largest group or as the top scorer, all-defect has the same number of runs or fewer in every batch. So my writing differs from his algorithm in something that matters, which the paper does not say or I have misread, and I do not know what it is; the published version, which I have not seen, may say more. None of this is sealed, the played-out tournament was tested only by its maker (against exact payoffs and against a second writing of it), and all of it wants doing again.
